content: ISO 639-3 is an international standard that provides a comprehensive set of three-letter codes for the representation of languages. It builds upon the ISO 639-2 alpha-3 codes with the goal of encompassing all known natural languages, including those that are living, extinct, ancient, or constructed, as well as major and minor languages, whether written or unwritten. This standard was officially published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) on February 5, 2007. The primary purpose of ISO 639-3 is to support a wide range of applications, particularly in computer systems where the representation and support of multiple languages are required. It aims to enumerate languages as completely as possible, providing a more extensive inventory than its predecessors, ISO 639-1 and ISO 639-2. While ISO 639-1 and ISO 639-2 primarily focused on major languages frequently represented in global literature, ISO 639-3 extends its scope to include a broader range of languages. ISO 639-3 is a superset of ISO 639-1 and the individual languages listed in ISO 639-2. However, it is not a complete superset of ISO 639-2 because ISO 639-2 includes language collections, which are not part of ISO 639-3. Additionally, where both bibliographic (B) and terminological (T) codes exist in ISO 639-2, ISO 639-3 adopts the T-codes. The final version of ISO 639-3 contains 7,589 entries. The inventory of languages included in this standard is derived from multiple sources, such as the individual languages listed in ISO 639-2, modern languages documented in the 15th edition of Ethnologue, historical and ancient languages, artificial languages cataloged by Anthony Aristar at the Linguist List, and languages recommended during a public commenting period. The transition from ISO 639-1 to ISO 639-3 can be facilitated using the list of ISO 639-1 codes. Since ISO 639-3 uses three-letter alphabetic codes, the theoretical maximum number of languages that can be represented is 17,576 (26 × 26 × 26). However, due to reserved ranges, special codes, and B-only codes defined in ISO 639-2, 545 codes are unavailable for use in ISO 639-3, reducing the upper limit to 17,032. This limit decreases further when accounting for language collections defined in ISO 639-2 and those yet to be defined in ISO 639-5. In some cases, languages previously considered dialects under ISO 639-2 are treated as individual languages in ISO 639-3. For example, under ISO 639-2, ara represents generic Arabic, while ISO 639-3 distinguishes Standard Arabic (arb) as a separate language. Similarly, Norwegian (nor) in ISO 639-2 is divided into its two components, Nynorsk (nno) and Bokmål (nob), which were already present in ISO 639-2. ISO 639-3 excludes collective languages, which are codes in ISO 639-2 that represent groups of related languages rather than a specific language. These collective codes are not included in ISO 639-3, as the standard focuses on individual languages rather than language groupings.
